claim: More than a hundred thousand protein sequences are added to global sequence databases every day.
source: Every day, more than a hundred thousand protein sequences are added to global sequence databases (UniProt Consortium, 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citation to UniProt Consortium, 2019a

claim: Curators assess more than 60,000 papers each year for protein annotation.
source: While curators diligently extract annotations from the literature, assessing more than 60,000 papers each year (UniProt Consortium, 2019b), the time-consuming nature of this task means that only ~0.03% of publicly available protein sequences are manually annotated.
evidence: Supported by citation to UniProt Consortium, 2019b

claim: Only approximately 0.03% of publicly available protein sequences are manually annotated.
source: While curators diligently extract annotations from the literature, assessing more than 60,000 papers each year (UniProt Consortium, 2019b), the time-consuming nature of this task means that only ~0.03% of publicly available protein sequences are manually annotated.
evidence: Supported by citation to UniProt Consortium, 2019b

claim: BLAST was introduced in 1990 as a method for pairwise sequence comparisons.
source: Starting in the 1980s, methods such as BLAST (Altschul et al., 1990) relied on pairwise sequence comparisons, where a query protein is assumed to have the same function as highly similar sequences that have already been annotated.
evidence: Supported by citation to Altschul et al., 1990

claim: The PROSITE database was introduced in 1991 for cataloguing short amino acid motifs.
source: Signature-based approaches were later introduced, with the PROSITE database (Bairoch, 1991) cataloguing short amino acid 'motifs' found in proteins that share a particular function.

claim: Profile hidden Markov models (HMMs) were developed in the 1990s.
source: Subsequently, a crucial refinement of signature-based approaches was the development of profile hidden Markov models (HMMs) (Krogh et al., 1994; Eddy, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krogh et al., 1994 and Eddy, 1998

claim: Profile HMMs allow for longer signatures and fuzzier matching compared to earlier methods.
source: Critically, profile HMMs allow for longer signatures and fuzzier matching and are currently used to update popular databases such as Interpro and Pfam (Bateman et al., 2019; Blum et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bateman et al., 2019 and Blum et al., 2021

claim: One-third of bacterial proteins cannot be annotated with a function even computationally.
source: These computational modelling approaches have had great impact; however, one-third of bacterial proteins still cannot be annotated (even computationally) with a function (Price et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Price et al., 2018

claim: Current alignment-based approaches conduct entirely separate comparisons for each comparator sequence or model.
source: First, current approaches conduct entirely separate comparisons for each comparator sequence or model, and thus may not fully exploit the features shared across different functional classes.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about how alignment-based methods work

claim: Deep neural networks have recently transformed image recognition tasks.
source: Deep neural networks have recently transformed a number of labelling tasks, including image recognition – the early layers in these models build up an understanding of simple features such as edges, and later layers use these features to identify textures, and then entire objects.
evidence: Supported by general knowledge and citation to Carter et al., 2019

claim: ProteInfer employs deep dilated convolutional networks to learn the mapping between full-length protein sequences and functional annotations.
source: To address this challenge we employ deep dilated convolutional networks to learn the mapping between full-length protein sequences and functional annotations.
evidence: Direct statement about the method used in this work

claim: ProteInfer models are trained on Swiss-Prot, the manually curated portion of UniProt.
source: The resulting ProteInfer models take amino acid sequences as input and are trained on the well-curated portion of the protein universe annotated by Swiss-Prot (UniProt Consortium, 2019b).
evidence: Direct statement about training data with citation

claim: ProteInfer models reproduce curator decisions for a variety of functional properties across sequences distant from the training data.
source: We find that (1) ProteInfer models reproduce curator decisions for a variety of functional properties across sequences distant from the training data

claim: Attribution analysis shows that ProteInfer predictions are driven by relevant regions of each protein sequence.
source: (2) attribution analysis shows that the predictions are driven by relevant regions of each protein sequence

claim: ProteInfer models create a generalised mapping between sequence space and the space of protein functions.
source: (3) ProteInfer models create a generalised mapping between sequence space and the space of protein functions, which is useful for tasks other than those for which the models were trained.

claim: ProteInfer uses residual layers with dilated convolutions.
source: We use residual layers, in which the output of each layer is added to its input to ease the training of deeper networks (He et al., 2015), and dilated convolutions (Yu and Koltun, 2015), meaning that successive layers examine larger sub-sequences of the input sequence.
evidence: Description of model architecture with citations

claim: Natural protein sequences can vary in length by at least three orders of magnitude.
source: Since natural protein sequences can vary in length by at least three orders of magnitude, this pooling is advantageous because it allows our model to accommodate sequences of arbitrary length without imposing restrictive modelling assumptions or computational burdens that scale with sequence length.
evidence: Statement about protein sequence length variation

claim: Each ProteInfer model was trained for about 60 hours using the Adam optimizer on 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs.
source: Each model was trained for about 60 hr using the Adam optimiser (Kingma and Ba, 2015) on 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs with data parallelism (Jeffrey, 2012; Shallue et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of training procedure with citations

claim: Swiss-Prot proteins go through a six-stage curation process.
source: Each protein in Swiss-Prot goes through a six-stage process of sequence curation, sequence analysis, literature curation, family-based curation, evidence attribution, and quality assurance.

claim: EC numbers represent the function of an enzyme in a hierarchical classification system.
source: These cross-references include Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers, representing the function of an enzyme

claim: GO terms relate to a protein's molecular function, biological process, or subcellular localisation.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) terms relating to the protein's molecular function, biological process, or subcellular localisation

claim: The study uses two methods to split data into training and evaluation sets: random split and UniRef50 clustering.
source: We use two methods to split data into training and evaluation sets. First, a random split of the data allows us to answer the following question: suppose that curators had randomly annotated only 80% of the sequences in Swiss-Prot. How accurately can ProteInfer annotate the remaining 20%? Second, we use UniRef50 (Suzek et al., 2015) clustering to split the data to model a challenging use case in which an unseen sequence has low sequence similarity to anything that has been previously annotated.
evidence: Description of data splitting methodology with citation

claim: There are 8162 catalogued chemical reactions represented by EC numbers in the dataset.
source: These are drawn from a total of 8162 catalogued chemical reactions.
evidence: Statement about the number of EC numbers in the dataset

claim: At the optimal confidence threshold, the EC prediction model correctly predicts 96.7% of true labels with a false-positive rate of 1.4%.
source: At the corresponding confidence threshold, the model correctly predicts 96.7% of true labels, with a false-positive rate of 1.4%.

claim: BLASTp was able to achieve higher recall values than ProteInfer for lower precision values.
source: We found that BLASTp was able to achieve higher recall values than ProteInfer for lower precision values, while ProteInfer was able to provide greater precision than BLASTp at lower recall values.

claim: ProteInfer was able to provide greater precision than BLASTp at lower recall values.
source: We found that BLASTp was able to achieve higher recall values than ProteInfer for lower precision values, while ProteInfer was able to provide greater precision than BLASTp at lower recall values.

claim: The high recall of BLAST likely reflects that it has access to the entirety of the training set rather than having to compress it into neural network weights.
source: The high recall of BLAST is likely to reflect the fact that it has access to the entirety of the training set, rather than having to compress it into a limited set of neural network weights.
evidence: Interpretation based on reasoning about method differences

claim: The lack of precision in BLAST could relate to reshuffling of sequences during evolution.
source: In contrast, the lack of precision in BLAST could relate to reshuffling of sequences during evolution, which would allow a given protein to show high similarity to a trainining sequence in a particular subregion, despite lacking the core region required for that training sequence's function.

claim: Neural network methods learn different information about proteins compared to alignment-based methods.
source: These patterns suggest that neural network methods learn different information about proteins to alignment-based methods, and so a combination of the two provides a synergistic result.

claim: For labels that occurred less than five times in the training set, 58% of examples in the test set were correctly recalled with 88% precision.
source: In contrast, for sequence data we found that even for labels that occurred less than five times in the training set, 58% of examples in the test set were correctly recalled, while achieving a precision of 88%, for an F1 of 0.7 (Figure 3—figure supplement 12).
evidence: Performance metric from experimental results with reference to figure

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae fol1 (accession Q4LB35) catalyses three sequential steps of tetrahydrofolate synthesis using three different protein domains.
source: For example, Saccharomyces cerevisiae fol1 (accession Q4LB35) catalyses three sequential steps of tetrahydrofolate synthesis using three different protein domains (Figure 4A).
evidence: Example protein with known function referenced with figure

claim: Class activation mapping (CAM) was used to identify the sub-sequences responsible for model predictions.
source: To investigate what sequence regions the neural network is using to make its functional predictions, we used class activation mapping (CAM) (Zhou et al., 2015) to identify the sub-sequences responsible for the model predictions.
evidence: Description of method used with citation

claim: Separate regions of sequence cause the prediction of each enzymatic activity in bifunctional enzymes, corresponding to known functions.
source: We found that separate regions of sequence cause the prediction of each enzymatic activity, and that these regions correspond to the known functions of these regions (Figure 4B).
evidence: Result from CAM analysis with figure reference

claim: In 296 of 304 (97%) bifunctional enzyme cases, ProteInfer correctly predicted the ordering of domains.
source: We found that in 296 of 304 (97%) of the cases, we correctly predicted the ordering, though we note that the set of bifunctional enzymes for which this analysis is applicable is limited in its functional diversity (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Performance metric from domain ordering analysis

claim: InterProScan compares each sequence against more than 50,000 individual signatures.
source: Whereas InterProScan compares each sequence against more than 50,000 individual signatures and BLAST compares against an even larger sequence database, ProteInfer uses a single deep model to extract features from sequences that directly predict protein function.

claim: In the penultimate layer of ProteInfer, each protein is expressed as a single point in a high-dimensional space.
source: One convenient property of this approach is that in the penultimate layer of the network each protein is expressed as a single point in a high-dimensional space.

claim: The ProteInfer embedding space captures the hierarchical nature of EC classification.
source: The resulting representation captures the hierarchical nature of EC classification, with the largest clusters in embedding space corresponding to top level EC groupings (Figure 5A).
evidence: Result from embedding analysis with figure reference

claim: Q8RUD6, annotated as Arsenate reductase (EC:1.20.4.1), was placed with sulfurtransferases (EC:2.8.1.-) rather than with other oxidoreductases.
source: For instance, Q8RUD6 is annotated as Arsenate reductase (glutaredoxin) (EC:1.20.4.1) (Chao et al., 2014) was not placed with other oxidoreductases (EC:1.-.-.-) but rather with sulfurtransferases (EC:2.8.1.-).
evidence: Observation from embedding analysis with citation

claim: Q8RUD6 can act as a sulfurtransferase.
source: Q8RUD6 can, however, act as a sulfurtransferase (Bartels et al., 2007).

source: This simple model achieved a precision of 97% and recall of 60% for an F1 score of 0.74.

claim: Model training and data-labelling for the membrane protein classifier took around 15 seconds.
source: Model training and data-labelling took around 15 s.

source: For example, the online interface to InterProScan can take 147 s to process a 1500 amino acid sequence (Protein used was Q77Z83. It should be noted that the individual databases that make up InterProScan may return matches faster, with the online interface to Pfam taking 14–20 s for a 1500 amino acid sequence.)

source: while running the tool may make the search faster, doing so requires downloading a 9 GB file, with an additional 14 GB for the full set of signatures, which when installed exceeds 51 GB.

claim: Conducting a BLAST search against Swiss-Prot takes 34 seconds for a 1500 amino acid sequence.
source: Meanwhile, conducting a BLAST search against Swiss-Prot takes 34 s for a 1500 amino acid sequence (a target database with decreased redundancy could be built to reduce this search time, and other optimisations of BLAST have been developed).

claim: The lightweight ProteInfer EC model is 5 MB and the GO model is 7 MB.
source: When the user loads the tool, lightweight EC (5 MB) and GO model (7 MB) prediction models are downloaded and all predictions are then performed locally, with query sequences never leaving the user's computer.

claim: Inference in the browser for a 1500 amino acid sequence takes less than 1.5 seconds for both EC and GO models.

claim: ProteInfer correctly classified Sinorhizobium meliloti protein Q92SI0 as a uridine nucleosidase (EC 3.2.2.3), while UniProt and InterProScan annotated it as Inosine-uridine nucleoside N-ribohydrolase (EC 3.2.2.1).
source: As an example, the Sinorhizobium meliloti protein Q92SI0 is annotated in UniProt as a Inosine-uridine nucleoside N-ribohydrolase (EC 3.2.2.1). Analysing the gene with InterProScan (Jones et al., 2014) also gives this prediction, but our model instead predicts it to be a uridine nucleosidase (EC 3.2.2.3), and this was indeed the result found in this experimental work.
